props.title: I Vitelloni

sections.content: I Vitelloni marks Federico Fellini's first masterpiece, revolutionizing the coming-of-age genre through its unflinching portrait of small-town ennui. Following five aimless young men in a provincial Italian coastal town, Fellini crafted a template that influenced countless films, from American Graffiti (1973) to Diner (1982). The film's DNA is evident in later works like The Last Picture Show (1971), where Peter Bogdanovich directly channeled Fellini's ability to capture the suffocating atmosphere of small-town life and arrested development.

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond Italy, creating a blueprint for exploring masculine immaturity that resonates through modern cinema. The Big Chill (1983) borrowed its structure of interconnected adult friendships, while Beautiful Girls (1996) directly homaged its winter carnival sequence. Even Martin Scorsese has cited I Vitelloni as a major influence on Mean Streets (1973), particularly in its portrayal of young men unable to escape their environment.

Fellini's innovative use of episodic storytelling and character vignettes established a narrative style that would define his later works like 8½ (1963) and Amarcord (1973). The film's treatment of Alberto, the mama's boy played brilliantly by Alberto Sordi, created a character archetype that would appear in countless Italian films, including Il Posto (1961) and The Easy Life (1962). sections.content: While rooted in Italian Neorealism, I Vitelloni marked a crucial transition point where directors began moving beyond pure social commentary toward more personal storytelling. This shift influenced the French New Wave, particularly François Truffaut's The 400 Blows (1959) and Federico Fellini's later work like La Dolce Vita (1960), which further developed the theme of privileged aimlessness.
